23445d8c60d2.t: The 12 Steps of AA: A Big Book Guide (Pages 58-60)

c4b1395eb2bd.t: The Twelve Steps as the Big Book presents them on pages 58-60, plus a plain-language guide to each step. Start with Step One and work forward.

eb9b449dda7d.t: The program of recovery exactly as pages 58 to 60 lay it out, one step at a time.

c11a7ba35d67.t: The Twelve Steps are not a list someone wrote for us to admire. They are the path the first members of Alcoholics Anonymous actually took to get sober, written down in Chapter 5 of the Big Book, <0>How It Works</0>. The chapter opens with a promise many of us have heard read aloud at meetings: 'Rarely have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path' (page 58). The steps themselves appear on pages 59 and 60, introduced simply as the steps the first members took, 'suggested as a program of recovery' (page 59). Suggested, not commanded. But the book is honest about what half-hearted effort gets us: 'Half measures availed us nothing. We stood at the turning point' (page 59).

62abaa125086.t: Read in order, the steps tell one story. We admit we are beaten (Step One), come to believe help exists (Step Two), and decide to accept it (Step Three). Then we get honest about our past (Steps Four and Five), let go of what blocks us (Six and Seven), repair the damage we caused (Eight and Nine), and build a daily life of inventory, prayer, and service (Ten, Eleven, and Twelve). Right after listing them, the book boils the whole program down to three ideas on page 60: we could not manage our own lives, probably no human power could relieve our alcoholism, and God could and would if He were sought.

0e461b5a7aa9.t: Many of us looked at that list and balked. The book saw us coming: many of us exclaimed, 'What an order! I can't go through with it.' (page 60). Its answer is the sentence that has steadied alcoholics for generations: 'We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection' (page 60). No one works these steps flawlessly. We simply stay 'willing to grow along spiritual lines' (page 60), and we start where every one of us started, with Step One. The guides below walk through each step the way the Big Book presents it, page by page, in plain language. Pick a step and begin.

153529a9fc5b.t: What are the 12 Steps of AA?

4156b634c23f.t: The Twelve Steps are the program of recovery described in the book Alcoholics Anonymous, listed on pages 59 and 60 of the 4th Edition. They move from admitting powerlessness over alcohol in Step One, through a moral inventory and making amends, to prayer, meditation, and carrying the message to other alcoholics in Step Twelve. The book presents them as the steps its first members took, 'suggested as a program of recovery' (page 59).

e93f26728cdd.t: Do you have to work the 12 Steps in order?

74ef728e6f09.t: The Big Book presents the steps as a sequence because each one builds on the honesty and willingness of the one before it. Step Four's inventory follows the decision made in Step Three, and the amends of Step Nine depend on the list made in Step Eight. Most of us work them in order with a sponsor, remembering the book asks only for spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection (page 60).

611ec027251e.t: Step 1 AA — Powerlessness Explained | Big Book Guide

c33eca448b07.t: Step 1 of AA explained from the Big Book: what powerless and unmanageable really mean, where the Step lives in the text, and how to take it, page by page.

7e17cc11333b.t: Step One is stated on page 59 of the Big Book, at the top of the list offered as a program of recovery: 'We admitted we were powerless over alcohol—that our lives had become unmanageable.' Every other Step stands on this one. The book puts the requirement plainly in More About Alcoholism: 'We learned that we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics. This is the first step in recovery' (page 30). Notice how high that bar sits. Not suspect it. Not say it out loud at a meeting while privately keeping an escape hatch open. Fully concede, to our innermost selves. Step One is taken when the argument inside us is over.

a6c75feab600.t: What Powerless Means in Big Book Terms

fb7df9810374.t: The Big Book describes alcoholism as a two-part problem, and powerless covers both parts. The first is physical. The Doctor's Opinion (pages xxv to xxxii) describes an allergy of the body: once alcohol is in the system, a craving develops that is limited to alcoholics and never occurs in the average temperate drinker (page xxviii). That is why the count of drinks never holds. The second part is mental, and it is the one that does the real damage. Page 24 tells us the real alcoholic has 'lost the power of choice in drink.' The memory of last month's humiliation does not surface with enough force when the thought of a drink arrives. 'We are without defense against the first drink' (page 24). And page 30 names the engine underneath it all: 'The idea that somehow, someday he will control and enjoy his drinking is the great obsession of every abnormal drinker.' Powerless is not an insult. It is a factual description: a body that cannot handle alcohol and a mind that cannot leave it alone.

ab1e6c4b4e92.t: Unmanageable is the second half of the admission, and it follows from the first. When drinking runs on that cycle of craving and obsession, life organizes itself around the problem. Jobs, money, marriages, health, and self-respect take their turns going sideways. But the deeper unmanageability is internal. Chapter 2 describes the point where even the most powerful desire to stop drinking is of no avail (page 24). We could not manage our own thinking about alcohol, so we could not manage the life that thinking kept producing.

70be1bc1fd16.t: Where Step One Lives in the Text

d079236f9555.t: Although the Step itself appears on page 59, the whole front of the book is Step One material. The Doctor's Opinion (pages xxv to xxxii) gives the medical picture of the allergy and the craving. Bill's Story (pages 1 to 16) shows one man living it out. There Is a Solution (pages 17 to 29) explains why willpower and self-knowledge fail us at the critical moment. And More About Alcoholism (pages 30 to 43) is the Step One chapter proper; its stated job is to smash the delusion that we are like other people. If you are working Step One, those pages are the assignment.

e75c8c73e36d.t: How the Big Book Has Us Work It

8b360dfddf4c.t: There is no worksheet for Step One in the Big Book. The instruction is self-diagnosis through rigorous honesty. First, the book invites us to test the facts rather than argue them: pages 31 and 32 suggest that anyone unsure of his condition try some controlled drinking, try to stop abruptly, and try it more than once, then judge the results honestly. Most of us had run that experiment for years without calling it one. Second, it hands us a plain diagnostic: 'If, when you honestly want to, you find you cannot quit entirely, or if when drinking, you have little control over the amount you take, you are probably alcoholic' (page 44). Third, it sets the standard: full concession, deep down, nothing held back (page 30). What changes when we do this? The fight ends. We stop spending ourselves proving we can drink safely and become teachable. The book warns that 'Half measures availed us nothing' (page 59), and Step One is where we stop taking half measures with the truth.

d9412c1d540b.t: Here is the honest part. Nearly everyone balks at this Step, because admitting powerlessness sounds like admitting we are weak, or finished, or less than other people. Many of us had built an identity on being the one who could handle things, and Step One felt like signing the papers on our own defeat. The experience of those who have taken it is the opposite. The admission does not end anything except an exhausting performance. We had already lost the fight; Step One simply stops us from pretending otherwise, and the pretending was the thing keeping us sick. There is real relief on the far side, the kind that comes from finally setting down something too heavy to carry.

e90d48b4c261.t: Step One leaves us with a problem fully admitted and still unsolved, and the book means to leave us there for a moment. 'Lack of power, that was our dilemma' (page 45). If we are powerless, then help has to come from somewhere beyond our own resources. That is exactly where Step Two picks up: 'Came to believe that a Power greater than ourselves could restore us to sanity' (page 59). First we admit that we cannot. Then we begin to look, honestly and without dread, at what can.

966c5c04ae3f.t: What does 'powerless over alcohol' mean in Step 1 of AA?

5926f78eb9d1.t: In the Big Book it means two specific things: a physical craving that starts once alcohol is in the body, described in The Doctor's Opinion (page xxviii), and a mental obsession that returns when we are sober. Page 24 says the real alcoholic has 'lost the power of choice in drink.' It is a description of a condition, not a judgment of character.

dc509efed1b1.t: How do I actually work Step 1 from the Big Book?

647f6bb63f7c.t: Read The Doctor's Opinion through More About Alcoholism (pages xxv to 43) and check your own drinking history against what they describe. The book's own test appears on pages 31 and 32: try some controlled drinking, more than once, and judge the results honestly. Step One is taken when you can fully concede to your innermost self that you cannot control alcohol and that life built around it has become unmanageable (page 30).

54088c52c95a.t: Step 10 AA — Continued Personal Inventory | Big Book Guide

bceab8fa5f8d.t: Step 10 of AA asks us to keep a continued personal inventory. See how the Big Book's pages 84-85 instruct it and what changes when we work it daily.

023ec34e8d73.t: The daily practice that keeps clean what Steps Four through Nine cleaned up.

31dec288122a.t: Step 10 is the moment the program stops being a project and becomes a way of life. The Big Book lists it on page 59: "Continued to take personal inventory and when we were wrong promptly admitted it." By the time we reach this Step we have cleaned house through Steps Four through Nine. Step 10 asks us to keep it clean. Page 84 introduces it as the practice of continuing our inventory and setting right new mistakes as we make them, right as we go along. We are not asked to relive the Fourth Step every morning. We are asked to notice today's mess today, while it is still small enough to fix with a sentence instead of an amends list.

99588eed0637.t: Where Step 10 Lives in the Big Book

98f2133cd192.t: The Step itself appears in the Twelve Steps on page 59, in the chapter "How It Works." The working instructions come near the end of "Into Action," on pages 84 and 85, immediately after the Ninth Step Promises. That placement is no accident. The book has just finished describing a life we could hardly have imagined, and without taking a breath it tells us how to keep it. Page 84 says we have entered the world of the Spirit, and that our next job is to grow in understanding and effectiveness. Then it sets the timeline: "This is not an overnight matter. It should continue for our lifetime" (page 84). Step 10 is not a chore bolted onto recovery. It is what recovery looks like from here forward.

e16b13ff768f.t: How the Big Book Says to Work It

09ed6a6d25a3.t: The instructions on page 84 are short enough to memorize and specific enough to use before lunch. "Continue to watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear" (page 84). Those are the same four troublemakers we hunted in the Fourth Step, and the book treats them as symptoms to catch, not sins to punish. When they crop up, the instruction is to ask God at once to remove them, to talk them over with someone right away, and to set things right quickly if anyone has been harmed. Then we turn our thoughts, resolutely, to someone we can help (page 84). Notice the tempo of those directions: <0>at once</0>, <1>immediately</1>, <2>quickly</2>, <3>promptly</3>. Step 10 is a speed Step. The old way was to let a resentment marinate for ten years. The new way is to catch it before dinner. The whole attitude fits in one short line: "Love and tolerance of others is our code" (page 84).

e1b8cf4ed134.t: What Changes When We Practice It

337b5329700d.t: Right after the instructions, the book hands us some of its boldest promises. "And we have ceased fighting anything or anyone—even alcohol" (page 84). Sanity has returned. "If tempted, we recoil from it as from a hot flame" (page 84). The reaction becomes automatic, given to us rather than manufactured by willpower. "We feel as though we had been placed in a position of neutrality—safe and protected" (page 85). The problem has been removed. But the same page carries a warning we ignore at our peril: "It is easy to let up on the spiritual program of action and rest on our laurels. We are headed for trouble if we do, for alcohol is a subtle foe" (page 85). The book is blunt about why: "We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (page 85). Read that carefully. The safety is real, and it is conditional. <0>Step 10 is the maintenance the reprieve depends on.</0>

c5300a659cad.t: The Honest Fear About This Step

22b04768e51b.t: Now the honest part. Most of us hear Step 10 and feel tired before we start. A lifetime of daily inventory sounds like living under a microscope, and promptly admitting we are wrong sounds like signing up to lose every argument forever. Some of us quietly fear becoming a doormat, apologizing our way through life. But the book never asks us to grovel, and it specifically cautions us not to drift into worry, remorse, or morbid reflection, because that would diminish our usefulness to others (page 86). It asks us to watch for four specific things and deal with them fast, the way we would patch a small leak before it floods the basement. In practice, promptly admitting a wrong is lighter than the alternative, which is carrying it. We spent years defending positions we knew were indefensible, and that was the exhausting life. Ten minutes of honesty costs less than ten days of resentment, and the Step immediately spends the saved energy on someone we can help (page 84).

b5b7bbadd28a.t: Step 10 keeps the slate clean through the day. Step 11 shows us how to open and close it. The book moves straight on: "Step Eleven suggests prayer and meditation" (page 85), and the nightly review on page 86 grows naturally out of the habit Step 10 has already built. If Step 10 is the maintenance of our new life, Step 11 is its power source. When today's inventory is done, turn the page with us.

c904bb312281.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition. Step 10 listed on p. 59 ("How It Works"); working instructions and Tenth Step promises pp. 84-85 ("Into Action"); daily reprieve warning p. 85; nightly review and Step 11 introduction pp. 85-86.

76ad33132ee6.t: How do I do a Step 10 inventory every day?

edc9c82be1ef.t: The Big Book's instructions are on page 84: continue to watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear. When they crop up, ask God at once to remove them, discuss them with someone immediately, and make amends quickly if anyone was harmed, then turn your thoughts to someone you can help. It is a continuous practice carried through the day, not only a written list at night; the evening review described on page 86 grows out of the same habit.

fdbda347fa68.t: What are the Step 10 promises in the Big Book?

f16dc6b03c76.t: On pages 84 and 85 the book says we have ceased fighting anything or anyone, even alcohol; sanity returns, we recoil from liquor as from a hot flame, and we feel placed in a position of neutrality, safe and protected. Page 85 adds the condition: this lasts only so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition, because what we have is a daily reprieve, not a cure.

2560fb2aaeb7.t: Step 11 AA — Prayer and Meditation | Big Book Guide

d4f81226c372.t: Step 11 in AA's Big Book explained: prayer and meditation on pages 85-88 of Into Action, plus how to work it morning, night, and all through the day.

2fa1bb19202f.t: How the Big Book teaches us to improve conscious contact with God, one morning, one evening, one pause at a time.

1433a2307763.t: Step 11 reads: 'Sought through prayer and meditation to improve our conscious contact with God as we understood Him, praying only for knowledge of His will for us and the power to carry that out' (page 59). Notice the word <0>improve</0>. The Big Book assumes that by now we already have some conscious contact. If we have worked the first ten Steps, page 85 tells us we have begun to sense the flow of God's Spirit into us and to develop what it calls a vital sixth sense. Step 11 is how we keep that connection alive and growing instead of letting it fade.

e3bc2e29378d.t: The stakes are spelled out on the same page. 'What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition' (page 85). We are not cured of alcoholism. The reprieve is renewed one day at a time, and prayer and meditation are the maintenance work. The housecleaning of Steps 4 through 9 opened a channel between us and God; Step 11 is how we keep it open.

4211751639af.t: Where Step 11 Lives in the Big Book

bf4e1c634ea5.t: The Step itself appears in the famous list on page 59, in the chapter 'How It Works.' The instructions for actually working it come near the end of Chapter 6, 'Into Action,' on pages 85 through 88. It is a short passage, barely three pages, but the book is not casual about it. 'It would be easy to be vague about this matter. Yet, we believe we can make some definite and valuable suggestions' (page 86). What follows is one of the most practical stretches of writing in the whole book: a simple routine for night, morning, and all the hours in between.

3b4ac0b908c0.t: How the Big Book Says to Work Step 11

60e859a63817.t: The routine starts at night. 'When we retire at night, we constructively review our day' (page 86). We ask the inventory questions: 'Were we resentful, selfish, dishonest or afraid?' (page 86). Do we owe an apology? Were we thinking mostly of ourselves, or of what we could pack into the stream of life? The book adds a gentle warning here. We must not drift into worry, remorse, or morbid reflection, because that would diminish our usefulness to others (page 86). After the review we simply ask God's forgiveness and ask what corrective measures should be taken.

a52f592da6a3.t: The morning gets its own instructions. 'On awakening let us think about the twenty-four hours ahead' (page 86). We consider our plans for the day and ask God to direct our thinking, especially asking that it be kept clear of self-pity and dishonest or self-seeking motives (page 86). When we face indecision, we ask God for inspiration, an intuitive thought or a decision, and then we relax and stop struggling (page 86). We usually close the meditation with a prayer that we be shown our next step through the day, asking especially for freedom from self-will and taking care never to pray for our own selfish ends (page 87).

f48ed3900496.t: Then the Step goes portable. 'As we go through the day we pause, when agitated or doubtful, and ask for the right thought or action' (page 87). We remind ourselves that we are no longer running the show, humbly repeating 'Thy will be done' (page 88) many times a day. That one pause, taken in traffic or mid-argument, is Step 11 in its working clothes.

193b881a488b.t: The book is specific about the payoff. Living this way, we are in much less danger of excitement, fear, anger, worry, self-pity, or foolish decisions, and we stop burning up energy trying to arrange life to suit ourselves (page 88). Page 87 promises that what used to be the occasional hunch or inspiration gradually becomes a working part of the mind. Guidance stops feeling like a lightning strike and starts feeling like a quiet, reliable sense of the next right thing. The book closes the passage with one of its plainest sentences: 'It works—it really does' (page 88).

dd2acc62ec3f.t: If Prayer Feels Awkward or Fake

43fb5cb231d4.t: Let's be honest about the resistance, because most of us felt it. We did not know how to pray. We felt like hypocrites talking to a God we had doubted, ignored, or blamed. Meditation sounded like something for monks. The book saw us coming: 'Step Eleven suggests prayer and meditation. We shouldn't be shy on this matter of prayer' (page 85). It even tells those of us with no religious background that we are allowed to borrow. We can memorize a few set prayers, lean on helpful books, and 'Be quick to see where religious people are right. Make use of what they offer' (page 87). Remember, the Step says God <0>as we understood Him</0>. No eloquence is required. A clumsy, honest request for knowledge of His will counts, and in our experience it gets answered.

a4e8e720ec74.t: Step 11 is not the finish line. Right after telling us it works, the book says, 'But this is not all. There is action and more action' (page 88), and it points us straight ahead: the next chapter is entirely devoted to Step Twelve. Conscious contact was never meant to be a private treasure. The power we are given in the morning quiet has a purpose, and that purpose is Step 12, carrying this message to the alcoholic who still suffers.

472418b5d38b.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition: Step 11 listed on p. 59 ('How It Works'); working instructions in Chapter 6, 'Into Action,' pp. 85-88; forward pointer to Step Twelve on p. 88.

5365d0ba8334.t: Where is Step 11 in the Big Book?

8590ef79835e.t: Step 11 appears in the Twelve Step list on page 59, in the chapter 'How It Works.' The instructions for practicing it come near the end of Chapter 6, 'Into Action,' on pages 85 through 88, which lay out a nightly review, a morning meditation, and short pauses for guidance all through the day.

078c759f6199.t: How do I work Step 11 if I don't know how to pray?

e3046f8d5fb1.t: The Big Book says we shouldn't be shy on the matter of prayer (page 85), and it clearly expects beginners. Page 87 suggests memorizing a few set prayers, using helpful books, and learning from religious people where they are right. The Step itself says God as we understood Him, so a simple, honest request for knowledge of His will and the power to carry it out is enough.

7485095247cf.t: Step 12 AA — Carrying the Message | Big Book Guide

a5660c93f32d.t: Step 12 AA explained with the Big Book: what the spiritual awakening means, how Chapter 7 says to carry the message, and how to live the principles.

abcc53f70743.t: The awakening was given to us so we could give it away.

031c176779c1.t: Step 12 reads: <0>'Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics, and to practice these principles in all our affairs'</0> (page 60). This is the harvest step. The first eleven Steps grew something in us, and this one tells us what to do with the crop. There are three parts: an awakening we received, a message we carry, and a set of principles we practice everywhere.

ff9dbf9e68a7.t: Notice the wording. The Step does not tell us to go find a spiritual awakening. It says we have had one, <0>as the result of these steps</0>. The awakening is not an entrance requirement; it is the natural outcome of work already done. Many of us worried that nothing dramatic had happened to us. The book answers that worry in Appendix II, explaining that most of our spiritual experiences are of the 'educational variety' that develops slowly over time (page 567). The real test is a personality change deep enough to bring about recovery, and it arrives in many forms (page 567). If we can stay sober today and honestly care about another human being, something real has happened to us. Page 25 describes the change as being lifted into a dimension of living we had never dreamed of.

4d29d3423f3b.t: Where Step 12 Lives in the Big Book

411452f8d737.t: The Step itself is listed on page 60, but its home is Chapter 7, 'Working With Others,' which runs from page 89 through page 103. That chapter is the Big Book's instruction manual for this Step. The closing lines of 'A Vision for You' belong here too, where the book tells us to 'Give freely of what you find and join us' (page 164). Appendix II, 'Spiritual Experience,' on pages 567 and 568, explains the awakening itself. And the 'all our affairs' portion reaches into the chapters on family and work that follow, because these principles are meant for our kitchens and our job sites, not only for Twelfth Step calls.

6af33b12544e.t: Chapter 7 opens with one of the most confident sentences in the whole book: 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics' (page 89). Then it adds, 'It works when other activities fail' (page 89). The instructions that follow are practical. Learn what you can about the person you hope to help, and do not exhaust yourself on someone who does not want to stop drinking (page 90). See him alone if possible, and lead with your own story rather than a lecture (page 91). Speak freely about the spiritual side in everyday language, and if he believes differently than you do, let him (page 93). Never preach and never push; if he is not interested, leave the door open for another day (page 95). Help in practical ways, but never do for him what he can do for himself (pages 96 through 98). Then comes the anchor of the whole chapter: 'Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery' (page 97). As for practicing these principles in all our affairs, page 83 says it without softening: 'The spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it.' Honesty in our paperwork, patience at the dinner table, kindness toward the person who irritates us most. That is Step 12 on an ordinary Tuesday.

f11c7ec3d85d.t: What Changes, and Where We Go From Here

d3226abb03b9.t: The promises attached to this Step are specific. 'Life will take on new meaning' (page 89). We watch people recover, we see them help others, we watch loneliness vanish, and a fellowship grows up around us. The book calls frequent contact with newcomers 'the bright spot of our lives' (page 89). The protection is real too, because the same page insists that nothing shields us from drinking like this work. Sobriety that once felt like gripping a rope starts to feel like standing on solid ground.

a73271a93784.t: Here is the honest part. Almost all of us balk at this Step for the same reason: we feel unqualified. Who are we to carry a message? Our awakening feels too quiet, our sobriety too new, and we are afraid of saying the wrong thing and driving someone away. The Big Book never asks us to be experts or preachers. It asks us to tell another alcoholic what happened to us, nothing more (page 91). The results were never our department anyway; we carry the message, not the alcoholic. And notice which direction the protection flows on page 89. We do this work as much for our own sobriety as for the newcomer's, so waiting until we feel ready gets it exactly backward.

6b7f960abc1d.t: Step 12 has no Step after it because it is not the top of a staircase; it is the door into a way of life. The daily practice of Steps 10, 11, and 12 keeps us fit, since what we have is a daily reprieve contingent on our spiritual condition (page 85), and the newcomer keeps us honest. Find the alcoholic who still suffers. Sit with her. Tell your story. The book promises that if our relationship with God is right, great events will come to pass for us and for countless others (page 164). We simply pass on what was so freely given to us.

6f8be482c8a2.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous, 4th ed.: Step 12 listed p. 60; 'Working With Others' pp. 89-103 (the Step 12 chapter); 'There Is a Solution' p. 25; 'Into Action' pp. 83, 85; 'A Vision for You' p. 164; Appendix II 'Spiritual Experience' pp. 567-568.

dd075898df66.t: What counts as a spiritual awakening in Step 12 of AA?

dd4e1704283f.t: The Big Book answers this in Appendix II (pages 567-568). Most awakenings are gradual, what the book calls the 'educational variety,' developing slowly over time rather than arriving in a flash of light. The test is a change in personality deep enough to bring about recovery. If you can stay sober and genuinely care about others, the awakening is already underway.

90b2a28a9cd6.t: How do I work Step 12 if I've never helped another alcoholic before?

78d267f83c67.t: Chapter 7, 'Working With Others' (pages 89-103), gives plain instructions: learn about the person, see them alone, tell your own story, and never preach (pages 90-95). You don't need to be an expert, because the message is simply what happened to you. Page 89 promises that nothing so insures immunity from drinking as this work, so it protects your own sobriety too.

8c1ce708f9ef.t: Step 2 AA — Came to Believe Explained | Big Book Guide

efbc411afafa.t: Step 2 of AA explained from the Big Book: what 'came to believe' means, where We Agnostics teaches it, and how to work the Step, with page citations.

723557724103.t: A little willingness, the Big Book promises, is enough to make a beginning.

f6e1b83eac56.t: Step Two reads, "Came to believe that a Power greater than ourselves could restore us to sanity" (page 59). Notice how gently that is worded. It does not say we believed, and it does not set a deadline for faith. It says we came to believe, the way we come to a place after walking toward it for a while. Step One left us with a real problem: we admitted we were powerless over alcohol. Step Two points to the only solution the Big Book offers, and it asks nothing up front except a little willingness.

0049e25b48f4.t: What Step Two Means in Big Book Terms

64d13ef2f7c8.t: The book names our situation plainly: "Lack of power, that was our dilemma. We had to find a power by which we could live, and it had to be a Power greater than ourselves" (page 45). The same page says the whole book's main object is to enable us to find that Power. So Step Two is not a side road for religious people. It is the hinge of the entire program. If willpower could have fixed us, Step One would never have been true.

a6d5d06813c8.t: The word sanity bothers many of us. But the Big Book means something specific. It says the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind rather than in his body (page 23). Then it tells the story of Jim, a man who reasoned that whiskey could not hurt him if he mixed it with milk, and concludes, "Whatever the precise definition of the word may be, we call this plain insanity" (page 37). The insanity of alcoholism is the strange failure of our defense against the first drink, the trivial excuse that sounds reasonable in the moment. To be restored to sanity is to get back the ability to see that first drink truthfully.

bc7af50b9ab0.t: Where Step Two Lives in the Text

af25682374e1.t: The Step appears in the list on page 59, in the chapter How It Works, but its home is We Agnostics, pages 44 through 57, a chapter written to the doubter by people who had been doubters themselves. The groundwork comes earlier. In Bill's Story, a sober friend at the kitchen table suggests Bill choose his own conception of God (page 12), and More About Alcoholism, pages 30 through 43, builds the case for the mental blank spot that needs restoring. Appendix II, Spiritual Experience, completes the picture on pages 567 and 568.

12386ac550e0.t: The instruction is surprisingly small. We ask ourselves one question: "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (page 47). The moment we can say yes, even to the willingness alone, the book emphatically assures us we are on our way, and it says an effective spiritual structure can be built on that simple cornerstone (page 47). We do not have to adopt anyone else's conception of God. Our own conception, however inadequate, is sufficient to make a beginning (page 46). Bill found exactly that: "It was only a matter of being willing to believe in a Power greater than myself. Nothing more was required of me to make my beginning" (page 12).

3b8f60214562.t: Working the Step means laying aside prejudice long enough to express that willingness (page 46). It means facing the choice the book states so bluntly: "God either is, or He isn't. What was our choice to be?" (page 53). And it means weighing the evidence in the rooms around us. Page 52 describes the life we could not fix on our own, the broken relationships, the emotions we could not control, the misery and depression and fear. Then it delivers the verdict: "Our ideas did not work. But the God idea did" (page 52).

cbc885968cef.t: What Changes, and the Fear That Stops Us

e563d8e984fe.t: The first thing that changes is hope. When we become willing, the argument inside us quiets, and the energy we spent fighting starts going into recovery. Appendix II says most of us tap an unsuspected inner resource which we presently identify with our own conception of a Power greater than ourselves (page 568), and it names the price of admission: "Willingness, honesty and open mindedness are the essentials of recovery" (page 568). For most of us this change is educational and gradual. We come to believe by watching sanity return, one clear-headed morning at a time.

dd5ca1e10c05.t: Now the honest part. Many of us feared this Step because religion had hurt us, or bored us, or been used against us, and we assumed we were being asked to swallow somebody else's God whole. We were not. About half of AA's original fellowship were exactly that doubting type (page 44), and they recovered without surrendering their honesty. Nobody hands us a required God. We start with whatever we can honestly accept, a Power greater than ourselves, and we let experience do the convincing. The fear says believe or else. The book only says be willing, and watch.

7ce6dc67bea0.t: Once we can answer yes, or even an honest <0>I am willing</0>, we are ready for what follows. Step Three turns belief into a decision: "Made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him" (page 59). Coming to believe is the turn toward the light. Step Three is the first step into it.

c5f7d328407b.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition: 'Bill's Story' (page 12); 'There Is a Solution' (page 23); 'More About Alcoholism' (pages 30-43, esp. page 37); 'We Agnostics' (pages 44-57); 'How It Works' (page 59); Appendix II, 'Spiritual Experience' (pages 567-568).

6c647aa253b3.t: What does 'restore us to sanity' mean in Step 2 of AA?

2665d286717f.t: In Big Book terms the insanity is not general madness but the strange mental blank spot around the first drink. The book says the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind rather than in his body (page 23), and after Jim's story it calls that kind of thinking plain insanity (page 37). Being restored to sanity means getting back the ability to see the first drink truthfully, something willpower alone never gave us.

abe60bfb1fcd.t: Do I have to believe in God to work Step 2?

0faa8b025263.t: No. We Agnostics was written for exactly this reader, and about half of AA's original fellowship were of that doubting type (page 44). The book asks only one question, whether we now believe or are even willing to believe that there is a Power greater than ourselves (page 47), and it says our own conception, however inadequate, is sufficient to make a beginning (page 46).

6c36612d93b2.t: Step 3 AA — Made a Decision | Big Book Guide

a5c3d29597a5.t: Step 3 of AA asks for a decision, not perfect surrender. We walk through how pages 60 to 63 of the Big Book instruct us to take it and what changes after.

7dde300eadab.t: Made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him.

6b0888f1812b.t: Step 3 reads: "Made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him." Notice what it asks for: a decision, not a lifetime of perfect surrender delivered in advance. In Step 1 we admitted we were beaten. In Step 2 we came to believe a Power greater than ourselves could restore us. In Step 3 we decide to let that Power go to work. Page 60 sets the stage with three plain convictions: that we were alcoholic and could not manage our own lives, that probably no human power could have relieved our alcoholism, and "That God could and would if He were sought." Convinced of those three things, we were at Step 3 (page 60).

150ad9c1d4ce.t: The phrase <0>as we understood Him</0> is the wide-open door of this program. The book is direct: "When, therefore, we speak to you of God, we mean your own conception of God" (page 47). Bill W. received that same gift when his friend Ebby asked, "Why don't you choose your own conception of God?" (page 12). Nobody hands us a theology. We start where we are, with whatever honest conception we can manage, and we make a decision.

7cc86f6c6b7a.t: Where Step 3 Lives in the Big Book

6f4aeac2c5b7.t: The Step appears on page 59, in Chapter 5, "How It Works," and the instructions run from page 60 through 63, with the handoff to Step 4 on page 64. The groundwork was laid one chapter earlier: "We Agnostics" (pages 44 through 57) clears away the religious objections before we arrive here, and Appendix II reminds us that willingness, honesty, and open-mindedness are the essentials of recovery (page 568). If Step 3 feels too big, those pages are the runway.

3746a5c58aca.t: How the Big Book Instructs Us to Work It

0df8f4dbc28f.t: The book begins with a diagnosis, not instructions. Any life run on self-will can hardly be a success, it tells us on page 60, then paints the actor who wants to run the whole show (pages 60 and 61). The verdict lands on page 62: "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles." In case we thought this described someone else, the same page adds, "The alcoholic is an extreme example of self-will run riot, though he usually doesn't think so" (page 62).

e22141d9d24f.t: The remedy follows at once. "First of all, we had to quit playing God. It didn't work" (page 62). Next we decided God was going to be our Director in this drama of life. "He is the Principal; we are His agents" (page 62). That is the whole shape of Step 3: we resign as general manager of the universe. Page 63 suggests taking this step with an understanding person, such as a spouse, close friend, or spiritual adviser, though it adds it is better to meet God alone than with someone who might misunderstand. Then comes the Third Step Prayer, which begins, "God, I offer myself to Thee—to build with me and to do with me as Thou wilt. Relieve me of the bondage of self, that I may better do Thy will" (page 63). The book adds, "The wording was, of course, quite optional so long as we expressed the idea, voicing it without reservation" (page 63). The idea, voiced without reservation. That is the work.

1d0a007c47d4.t: What Changes When We Make the Decision

5d93e20087b1.t: Page 63 does not oversell the result or undersell it. "When we sincerely took such a position, all sorts of remarkable things followed." We had a new Employer, the book says, who provided what we needed when we kept close to Him and did His work well. We became less interested in ourselves and our little plans, and more interested in what we could contribute to life (page 63). As new power and peace flowed in, we began to lose our fear of today, tomorrow, and the hereafter. "We were reborn" (page 63). The book is honest that this is only a beginning, though an effect, sometimes a very great one, is felt at once (page 63).

32c83d17cdb9.t: Here is the fear, said plainly: if I turn my will and my life over, I will lose myself. God will take away everything I enjoy, enroll me in a religion I never chose, and run my life like a warden. But look at the actual words of the Step. We turn our lives over to the <0>care</0> of God, and care is what a shepherd gives, not a jailer. Step 1 already taught us we were never really in control; our best managing landed us here (page 60). We are not giving up control we possess; we are stopping the pretense that we possess it. The only thing Step 3 costs us is the exhausting job of playing God, and page 62 already told us how that job was going.

30780393cb93.t: One warning, and one direction. The book says on page 64 that our decision, vital and crucial as it was, could have little permanent effect unless followed at once by a strenuous effort to face the things in ourselves that had been blocking us. A decision without action fades. So we do not sit and admire Step 3; we launch into vigorous action, a searching personal inventory. It is called Step 4.

2a2125cb8e62.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition — Chapter 5 "How It Works" pp. 58-64 (Step 3 text p. 59; instructions pp. 60-63; Third Step Prayer p. 63; bridge to Step 4 p. 64); Chapter 4 "We Agnostics" pp. 44-57; Chapter 1 "Bill's Story" p. 12; Appendix II "Spiritual Experience" pp. 567-568.

e20d8ea7b195.t: What does Step 3 in AA actually mean?

6e86979bf59f.t: Step 3 is a decision, not a finished act of surrender. The Big Book says our root trouble is selfishness and self-centeredness (page 62), so we decide to stop running our lives on self-will and let God direct them instead (page 62). The phrase 'as we understood Him' means we start with our own conception of God (page 47), not anyone else's.

20838f234125.t: How do I take Step 3 using the Big Book?

5420eb15cf57.t: Pages 60 through 63 lay it out. First we get convinced that a life run on self-will cannot succeed (page 60), then we make the decision, ideally with an understanding person — the book suggests a wife, best friend, or spiritual adviser (page 63), and today many of us take it with a sponsor — or alone with God, since the book says it is better to meet God alone than with someone who might misunderstand (page 63). Many of us use the Third Step Prayer on page 63, but the book says the wording is optional as long as we express the idea without reservation. Then we move promptly into the Step 4 inventory (page 64).

171fa7313b84.t: Step 4 AA — Searching and Fearless Inventory | Big Book Guide

fb208d03ffb2.t: Step 4 AA is explained from the Big Book: what the searching and fearless moral inventory means, how pages 63-71 say to write it, and what changes.

f3e58731598a.t: Step 4: Searching and Fearless Moral Inventory

c88d6a511ed3.t: The Big Book's written housecleaning: resentment, fear, and honesty, one column at a time.

a94a0d20c6f9.t: Step 4 reads: 'Made a searching and fearless moral inventory of ourselves' (page 59). The word moral makes a lot of us flinch, but the Big Book is not describing a courtroom. It is describing a stock-taking. As it says on page 64, 'A business which takes no regular inventory usually goes broke.' We do the same thing with our lives. Step 3 was a decision, and the book warns it moves nothing unless we follow it at once with strenuous effort to face what has been blocking us (page 64). Then comes the sentence that reframes the whole program: 'Our liquor was but a symptom. So we had to get down to causes and conditions' (page 64). Step 4 is where we go looking for those causes, on paper, with nothing left out.

d8d229d6fe5a.t: Where Step 4 Lives in the Big Book

a7ee2bb26820.t: Step 4 appears in the list of the Twelve Steps on page 59, and its working instructions fill the second half of Chapter 5, 'How It Works,' from page 63 through page 71. Within 'How It Works,' Step 4 gets more sustained instruction than any Step before it — nearly eight pages of concrete directions. There is even a sample inventory grid printed on page 65 so we can see exactly what the finished work looks like. If we have ever wondered whether the Big Book gives concrete directions or just inspiration, this is the section that settles it. There are columns to fill in, questions to answer, and prayers to say, all laid out in order.

ff7cb9af3b28.t: How the Big Book Says to Work Step 4

dcce4106d240.t: The inventory covers three areas: resentment, fear, and sex conduct. Resentment comes first because the book calls it the 'number one' offender and says it destroys more alcoholics than anything else (page 64). The instruction is plain: 'In dealing with resentments, we set them on paper' (page 64). We list every person, institution, and principle we are angry at, write down the cause, and then note which part of self was hurt, whether our self-esteem, our security, our ambitions, or our personal and sex relations (pages 64-65). The stakes are spelled out on page 66: 'If we were to live, we had to be free of anger.'

70faa4a39154.t: Then the book does something surprising. Instead of sending us after the people on our list, it asks us to see them as spiritually sick and to treat them the way we would treat a sick friend (pages 66-67). When someone offends, we say: 'This is a sick man. How can I be helpful to him? God save me from being angry. Thy will be done' (page 67). Only after that do we turn the pencil around. Putting the wrongs others have done out of our minds, we look for our own mistakes: 'Where had we been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking and frightened?' (page 67).

c88c6d203772.t: Fear gets its own review. The book calls fear 'an evil and corroding thread' running through the fabric of our existence (page 67), and the directions are just as concrete: 'We reviewed our fears thoroughly. We put them on paper, even though we had no resentment in connection with them' (page 68). We ask ourselves why we have them, and then we ask God 'to remove our fear and direct our attention to what He would have us be' (page 68). Last comes our sex conduct, reviewed with the same honesty, asking where we were selfish or dishonest and whom we hurt. The book says 'we tried to shape a sane and sound ideal for our future sex life' (page 69), asking God in meditation what to do about each specific matter.

21a7c901aaa1.t: What Changes When We Do It

5082854f81b2.t: Something shifts when a resentment moves from our head onto a page. We can finally see it whole, and we begin to see our own hand in it. The book says we begin to learn tolerance, patience, and good will toward everyone, even the people who hurt us, because we start seeing them as sick rather than as enemies (page 70). The chapter closes with quiet encouragement: 'If you have already made a decision, and an inventory of your grosser handicaps, you have made a good beginning' (page 71). We have 'swallowed and digested some big chunks of truth' about ourselves (page 71). That truth is not a burden. It is the raw material of freedom, because we cannot be rid of what we have never looked at.

3d5add56b8cb.t: The Fear of Starting, and What Comes Next

49694c1e3f62.t: Here is the honest part. Many of us stall at Step 4, some for months, some for years. We are afraid that if we write it all down, the page will prove what we secretly suspect, that we are beyond repair. But notice what the Step actually asks for: searching and fearless, not perfect. And notice this too: everything that ends up on the paper was already inside us, running the show in the dark. Writing it down does not make it worse. It makes it visible, and visible things can be dealt with. Nobody grades this inventory, and nobody sees it yet.

3adae4e08521.t: Sharing it is the next piece of work. With the inventory in hand, we turn to Step 5, where Chapter 6, 'Into Action,' begins on page 72: admitting to God, to ourselves, and to another human being the exact nature of our wrongs. The paper we just wrote is the map for that conversation.

8b776dd1d624.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition: p. 59 (Step Four in the Twelve Steps); Chapter 5, 'How It Works,' pp. 63-71 (inventory instructions: resentment pp. 64-67 with the sample grid on p. 65, fear pp. 67-68, sex conduct pp. 68-69, summary pp. 70-71); Chapter 6, 'Into Action,' p. 72 (Step Five).

c38c0f39ebef.t: How do I write a Step 4 inventory according to the Big Book?

b506dcf6698c.t: On paper, in columns. The Big Book says to list resentments first: who we are angry at, the cause, and which part of self it affects (pages 64-65). We then review our fears the same way (page 68) and our sex conduct (pages 68-69), then look for our own part in each area — for resentments, asking where we were selfish, dishonest, self-seeking, and frightened (page 67); for fears, asking why we had them (page 68); and for sex conduct, asking where we were selfish, dishonest, or inconsiderate and whom we hurt (page 69).

7f86c6bf8068.t: Why does Step 4 in AA start with resentment?

923bb4ebc749.t: Because the Big Book calls resentment the 'number one' offender and says it destroys more alcoholics than anything else (page 64). For people like us, anger is not a luxury we can afford; page 66 says that if we were to live, we had to be free of anger. Setting resentments on paper is how they begin to lose their grip.

63d803b6eb20.t: Step 5 AA — Admitting Our Wrongs | Big Book Guide

c3c10d6b0a4f.t: We explain Step 5 of AA from the Big Book: what admitting our wrongs means, how pages 72 to 75 instruct the Step, and what changes when we take it.

ddc4c91d6174.t: Step 5 reads: 'Admitted to God, to ourselves, and to another human being the exact nature of our wrongs' (page 59). If Step 4 was writing the inventory, Step 5 is reading it out loud. We take the resentments, fears, and harms we put down on paper and we admit them three ways: to God, to ourselves, and to one other person. The Big Book gives this Step only a few pages, but it does not treat it as optional. It calls it vital, and it tells us plainly what tends to happen to those who skip it.

be4949753229.t: Where Step 5 Lives in the Big Book

0d060c76f6e5.t: The Step itself appears in the list of the Twelve Steps on page 59, in the chapter <0>How It Works</0>. The working instructions open Chapter 6, <1>Into Action</1>, and run from page 72 through page 75. The chapter begins with a question: having made our personal inventory, what shall we do about it? The answer is Step 5, and the book gives its best reason first: 'If we skip this vital step, we may not overcome drinking' (page 72). Time after time, it says, newcomers tried to keep certain facts about their lives to themselves. They looked for easier methods, and almost invariably they got drunk. 'They took inventory all right, but hung on to some of the worst items in stock' (page 73). The housecleaning was started but never finished, so the house never came clean.

f6098c27332c.t: First we choose the person, and we choose carefully. Page 74 says that if we belong to a faith that requires confession, we go to the properly appointed authority. If not, we may talk with a minister, a doctor, a psychologist, or a close-mouthed, understanding friend. The person should be able to keep a confidence, understand what we are driving at, and not try to change our plan (page 74). One caution matters here: we cannot disclose anything that would hurt our wives or our parents, because we have no right to save our own skin at another person's expense. 'The rule is we must be hard on ourself, but always considerate of others' (page 74).

86107e1fdeda.t: Then we act. Once we decide who is to hear our story, we waste no time (page 75). We bring the written inventory, we explain what we are doing and why, and then, in one of the book's most vivid lines, 'We pocket our pride and go to it, illuminating every twist of character, every dark cranny of the past' (page 75). Withholding nothing is the whole instruction. Afterward we return home, find a quiet hour, thank God that we know Him better, and carefully review the first five Steps, asking if we have omitted anything. The book says we are building 'an arch through which we shall walk a free man at last' (page 75), and it asks us to check our own stonework.

38d1b9f47915.t: What Changes When We Take This Step

753bf4d28306.t: Page 75 describes the result in some of the warmest language in the book: 'We can look the world in the eye. We can be alone at perfect peace and ease. Our fears fall from us. We begin to feel the nearness of our Creator.' It goes on to say that we may have had certain spiritual beliefs before, but now we begin to have a spiritual experience, and the feeling that the drink problem has disappeared will often come strongly (page 75). That is not a reward for being good. It is what happens when a person stops carrying secrets alone.

a8b5f01c3e70.t: The Fear of Telling Another Person

96407e054ada.t: Let us be honest about the objection almost everyone raises: I have admitted this to myself and to God, so why drag another human being into it? The book answers that a solitary self-appraisal is usually insufficient (page 72), and it explains why. 'More than most people, the alcoholic leads a double life' (page 73). We presented a stage character to the world while pushing the worst memories down inside, and that constant fear and tension made for more drinking. The dread we feel before a Fifth Step is really the dread of ending the double life, and that is exactly why it works. 'We must be entirely honest with somebody if we expect to live long or happily in this world' (page 73). In practice, the person we tell is almost never shocked. Page 75 says most people approached this way are glad to help and feel honored by our confidence.

1629ad6d1c0f.t: When the review of our arch is done and the work feels solid, the book moves us straight ahead: 'If we can answer to our satisfaction, we then look at Step Six' (page 76). We have seen the exact nature of our wrongs and said them out loud. Step 6 asks whether we are entirely ready to have God remove them.

6ec2c8c3f0fc.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition: page 59 (How It Works, the Twelve Steps list); pages 72-75 (Into Action, Step 5 instructions); page 76 (transition to Step Six).

d01c79396a81.t: What page is Step 5 in the Big Book?

f68a8b430bec.t: Step 5 is listed with the other Twelve Steps on page 59, in the chapter How It Works. The instructions for actually working it open Chapter 6, Into Action, and run from page 72 through page 75, ending with a quiet hour of review before the book turns to Step 6 on page 76.

97bcc31cb827.t: Who should I do my Fifth Step with?

604f6be884f5.t: The Big Book suggests a properly appointed religious authority if our faith requires confession, or otherwise a minister, a doctor or psychologist, or a close-mouthed, understanding friend (page 74). The person should keep a confidence, understand what we are doing, and not try to change our plan. We are also cautioned not to share anything that would hurt family members, because we have no right to save our own skin at another person's expense (page 74).

4a8c319bf4a8.t: Step 6 AA — Entirely Ready | Big Book Guide

673b279a10b9.t: Learn what Step 6 of AA means in the Big Book: the page 76 instructions, what entirely ready really asks of us, and how willingness leads into Step 7.

da1e7370397a.t: Step Six reads: 'Were entirely ready to have God remove all these defects of character' (page 59). It is one of the shortest instructions in the whole program, and it is easy to hurry past. But Step Six is where the program stops being only about what we did while drinking and starts being about who we are. Steps Four and Five showed us the wreckage and the patterns behind it. Step Six asks a simple, searching question: now that we have seen these things clearly, are we willing to live without them? Notice that we do not remove anything ourselves. Our job is readiness. The removing belongs to God.

72961210a409.t: Where Step 6 Lives in the Big Book

f9e3081a1f15.t: The Step itself appears in the list of the Twelve Steps in the chapter How It Works (page 59). The instructions for working it come one chapter later, in Into Action, on page 76. The Big Book gives Step Six exactly one paragraph, and that brevity is not neglect. It is a signal that the work here is inward. The setup matters too. After Step Five, the Book has us return home, find a quiet hour, and review the first five Steps carefully, because 'we are building an arch through which we shall walk a free man at last' (page 75). We check our work the way a builder checks a foundation. Only when we are satisfied that those first five stones are solid do we look at Step Six.

bbc6b04defeb.t: The paragraph on page 76 opens plainly: 'We have emphasized willingness as being indispensable.' Then it puts a question to us: 'Are we now ready to let God remove from us all the things which we have admitted are objectionable?' It presses the point further, asking whether He can take them all, every single one (page 76). Read that slowly. The list of objectionable things did not come from a preacher or a pamphlet. It came from our own Fourth Step inventory and our own mouth in Step Five. We admitted these things ourselves. Step Six only asks whether we meant it.

c78fd85a2e95.t: Then comes the sentence that makes this Step workable for real human beings: 'If we still cling to something we will not let go, we ask God to help us be willing' (page 76). That is the entire method. We sit quietly with what the inventory showed us. We ask the question honestly. Where the answer is yes, we thank God. Where the answer is no, we do not fake it and we do not despair. We pray for the willingness we lack. The Book has already told us why we cannot simply fix ourselves; page 62 traces our troubles to their root: 'Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles.' A self-centered mind cannot uproot its own self-centeredness. So we ask for help becoming ready, the same way we asked for help getting sober.

318df5e91ddf.t: What Changes When We Become Entirely Ready

334e750bfa85.t: Something quiet but real shifts in Step Six. We stop defending the very things that have been beating us. For years we protected our resentments because they felt like justice, our fears because they felt like caution, our pride because it felt like dignity. Becoming entirely ready means we finally file them where the inventory said they belong: not as personality, but as the blocks standing between us and God and other people. This is the Third Step decision applied to our character. And it does not demand instant sainthood. Page 60 says it straight: 'We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection.' Entirely ready does not mean entirely fixed. It means nothing on the list is off the table anymore.

0b7b9386392e.t: Here is the honest part. Most of us reach Step Six and discover we still like some of our defects. Anger gets results. Pride feels like backbone. Worry feels responsible. Underneath sits a real fear: if God removes all of this, what is left of me? That fear deserves respect, not shame, and the Book quietly answers it. It never asks us to feel ready or to enjoy the prospect. It asks whether we are willing, and when we are not, it hands us one instruction: ask God to help us be willing (page 76). Willingness to become willing counts. What we cannot do is carve out a favorite defect and keep it on purpose, because page 59 already warned us that 'Half measures availed us nothing.'

c3928b4e1fdf.t: When we can answer with a wholehearted yes, or at least an honest prayer toward yes, the Book moves us straight ahead. The very next lines on page 76 give us Step Seven, where we humbly ask God to take what we have become ready to release. Step Six packs the bags. Step Seven hands them over.

a235fe551f29.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition — the Twelve Steps, pp. 59-60 (Chapter 5, How It Works); the root of our troubles, p. 62; reviewing our work and taking Steps Six and Seven, pp. 75-76 (Chapter 6, Into Action).

7119b21cd3de.t: Where is Step 6 in the Big Book?

debb398a4f6c.t: Step 6 is listed with the Twelve Steps on page 59, in the chapter How It Works. The instructions for working it are in the chapter Into Action, on page 76, where the Big Book gives it a single paragraph built around a searching question about willingness and a prayer for the willingness we lack.

0d852a260e4b.t: What if I'm not entirely ready to give up all my character defects?

694bcfda579c.t: The Big Book expects this. Page 76 says, 'If we still cling to something we will not let go, we ask God to help us be willing.' We are asked for willingness, not perfection; page 60 reminds us that we claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection, so an honest prayer for readiness is enough to keep moving.

122ccf5890de.t: Step 7 AA — Humbly Asking Explained | Big Book Guide

7d7e01f74f46.t: Step 7 of AA explained from the Big Book: what humbly asking God to remove our shortcomings means, the page 76 prayer, and how the Step is actually taken.

d16108648762.t: One paragraph, one prayer, and a new way of standing before God (page 76).

4cf4ed06d46d.t: Step 7 says: "Humbly asked Him to remove our shortcomings." That is the whole Step as the Big Book lists it on page 59, and it may be the shortest piece of work in the book. By the time we reach it we have written an inventory in Step 4, admitted the exact nature of our wrongs to God, to ourselves, and to another person in Step 5, and become entirely ready in Step 6 to have God remove what we found. Step 7 is simply where we ask. It occupies a single paragraph on page 76 of the chapter <0>Into Action</0>, and most of that paragraph is a prayer.

095764cf765c.t: What Step 7 Means in Big Book Terms

8eee4e9ffcc2.t: Our shortcomings are not a mystery by this point. They are the specific things our inventory turned up: resentment, which the Big Book calls the number one offender (page 64), along with fear, dishonesty, and selfish demands on the people around us. The book has already named the taproot: "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles" (page 62). Steps 6 and 7 share page 76 for a reason. Step 6 asks a readiness question: "Are we now ready to let God remove from us all the things which we have admitted are objectionable?" (page 76). Step 7 is what we do the moment the answer is yes. Notice who does the removing. We do not grit our teeth and self-improve. Having proved to ourselves in Step 1 that willpower could not solve our drinking, we do not expect it to solve our character either. We ask God, as we understand Him, to do for us what we could not do for ourselves.

d14d64e0a9cb.t: How the Big Book Tells Us to Take the Step

fd963801f940.t: The instruction on page 76 is disarmingly simple. "When ready, we say something like this" (page 76), the book tells us, and then gives the Seventh Step Prayer. We begin, "My Creator, I am now willing that you should have all of me, good and bad" (page 76). We ask Him to remove "every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to you and my fellows" (page 76). We finish, "Grant me strength, as I go out from here, to do your bidding" (page 76). Then comes the quiet closing line: "We have then completed Step Seven" (page 76). No ceremony, no waiting period, no committee approval.

416b89c86d1b.t: Two details in that prayer carry the whole meaning of the word <0>humbly</0>. First, we offer God all of ourselves, good and bad. Humility here is not groveling; it is honesty about our actual size, the same honesty we practiced in our inventory. Second, the measuring stick is <1>usefulness</1>. We do not ask to be made comfortable, admired, or flawless. We ask to have removed whatever blocks us from being useful to God and the people around us. That one word quietly reorders our ambitions. Notice also that the book says we pray something like this. The words are a pattern, not a magic formula. What matters is that we mean them.

d55397661b86.t: What Changes, and the Fear We Bring to This Step

50bfa65887ed.t: What changes first is direction. The prayer asks for strength to go out and do God's bidding, and the very next sentence on page 76 turns to action, reminding us that "Faith without works is dead" (page 76) and pointing straight at Steps 8 and 9. Step 7 is the hinge between the housecleaning we did on paper and the amends we now make in person. The removal of our defects then shows up in daily living rather than in a single lightning bolt. Page 84 shows the Step becoming a reflex. As we keep watching for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear, "When these crop up, we ask God at once to remove them" (page 84). We asked once on page 76; we keep asking for the rest of our lives, and we find that the asking works.

3838f20c0de4.t: Here is the honest part. Many of us fear this Step for two opposite reasons. Some of us secretly suspect our defects <0>are</0> our personality, and that if God removed them there would be nothing left, no edge, no humor, no drive. Others of us pray the prayer, catch ourselves resentful again by Thursday, and quietly conclude the Step failed. The Big Book answers both fears the same way. "We are not saints" (page 60), it says plainly, and "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection" (page 60). God does not remove our personhood; He removes what blocks it. And He does not seem to remove in one transaction what we are still half enjoying. Our part is willingness and asking. His part is the removing, on His schedule, usually in the measure that we walk into the action Steps that follow.

22ae13ac4e17.t: Which is exactly where the book sends us next. Step 8 asks us to make a list of all persons we had harmed and become willing to make amends to them all, and page 76 tells us the list is already in our hands: "We made it when we took inventory" (page 76). Humbly asked, we go out from here with work to do.

ed0999bdc5af.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition: p. 59 (Step Seven as listed in How It Works); pp. 60, 62, 64 (How It Works: progress not perfection, selfishness as root, resentment as number one offender); p. 76 (Into Action: Steps Six and Seven, the Seventh Step Prayer, transition to Steps Eight and Nine); p. 84 (Into Action: Step Ten, asking God at once to remove defects).

3dc48e224a38.t: What is the Seventh Step Prayer and what page is it on?

d41a55a83aca.t: The Seventh Step Prayer is on page 76 of the Big Book, in the chapter Into Action. We offer God all of ourselves, good and bad, ask Him to remove "every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to you and my fellows" (page 76), and ask for strength to do His bidding. The book introduces it as something we say, in words like these, so meaning the prayer matters more than reciting it perfectly.

2b4b946717b8.t: Are shortcomings and character defects different in AA?

2033dae60813.t: The Big Book treats them as the same things seen from the same inventory. Step 7 says shortcomings (page 59), Step 6 speaks of the things we have admitted are objectionable (page 76), and the Seventh Step Prayer asks God to remove every single defect of character (page 76). Different words, one list: the resentments, fears, selfishness, and dishonesty our Fourth Step uncovered.

e2a069e172e8.t: Step 8 AA Explained — The Amends List | Big Book Guide

f6183b6df3cd.t: Step 8 of AA explained from the Big Book: what the amends list means, where it lives on page 76, and how willingness comes even for the hardest names.

09f3b663b510.t: Step 8 says: "Made a list of all persons we had harmed, and became willing to make amends to them all." It stands eighth among the Twelve Steps on page 59 of the Big Book, and its working instructions live in Chapter 6, Into Action, beginning on page 76. This is a pencil-and-paper Step. Nobody gets called, nobody gets visited, and no doors get knocked on yet. We make a list, and we become willing. That is the whole assignment, and the Big Book builds a surprising amount of mercy into it.

f2b4d5b2b827.t: What Step 8 Says and Where It Lives in the Big Book

ffd91d3c33b9.t: Right after the Seventh Step Prayer on page 76, the book turns to the amends Steps with a reminder that "Faith without works is dead" (page 76). Then it says something that surprises many of us. Speaking of Steps Eight and Nine together, the book states, "We have a list of all persons we have harmed and to whom we are willing to make amends. We made it when we took inventory" (page 76). In other words, the Big Book does not treat Step 8 as a brand-new project. The Fourth Step inventory on pages 64 to 71 already surfaced the names. The people in our resentment column, the people tangled up in our fears, and the people we hurt in our sex conduct review are sitting right there in our own handwriting.

631026a4ebed.t: Working Step 8 has two motions. First, we make the list. We go back through our inventory and write down every person we actually harmed. The posture is the one the book taught us on page 67, where we were told, "Putting out of our minds the wrongs others had done, we resolutely looked for our own mistakes." That same discipline builds the amends list. A name goes on the list because we did damage, not because the other person was innocent. Many of the people we harmed also harmed us, and the book asks us to set that aside for now. We look for real harm: money owed, trust broken, promises abandoned, reputations dented, families frightened.

6161053ffea8.t: Second, we become willing. The book knows some names will stick in our throat, and it gives plain instructions for exactly that moment: "If we haven't the will to do this, we ask until it comes" (page 76). Willingness is not something we manufacture by gritting our teeth. We pray for it, and we keep praying until it arrives. The book also reminds us on the same page that we agreed at the beginning to go to any lengths for victory over alcohol. The list is one of those lengths.

6b6215c63fdf.t: The Fear That Stops Us Here

bfe72c183c80.t: Let's be honest about why so many of us stall at Step 8. The moment the list stops being an idea and becomes actual names, fear shows up. We are afraid of certain faces. We are afraid of what admitting harm might cost us in money, in pride, or in relationships we only barely repaired. And underneath it all is the old argument that half the people on the list hurt us worse than we ever hurt them. The Big Book does not scold us for any of this. It quietly separates the list from the action. Step 8 asks for willingness only; Step 9 will handle the doing, with careful guidance and timing of its own. Today we need nothing but paper, honesty, and the prayer on page 76 for willingness we do not yet have. That much we can do.

2a592e21db1d.t: What Changes, and Where This Leads

1208c5707f75.t: Something shifts when the wreckage of our past moves out of the fog and onto a single sheet of paper. The book describes the amends process as an attempt to sweep away the debris that piled up while we were living on self-will and running the show ourselves (page 76). A written list makes that debris finite. It has edges. It can be worked. Guilt that used to circle us at night becomes a set of names we are preparing, with God's help, to face. And the purpose behind it is bigger than tidying our own history. The book says, "Our real purpose is to fit ourselves to be of maximum service to God and the people about us" (page 77). The list is how we get fit.

1abcd93e1001.t: The Promises that follow the amends work include this one: "We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it" (page 83). That freedom starts with the list we write today. When the names are down and the willingness has come, even for the hard ones, we are ready for Step 9, where we go to the people we have harmed and set things right, directly wherever possible, except when doing so would injure them or others. The list is the map. Step 9 is the journey.

7b998fd9a62a.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition: page 59 (Step Eight as listed in How It Works); pages 76-77 (Into Action, working instructions for Steps Eight and Nine, sweeping away the debris, maximum service); pages 64-71 (the Fourth Step inventory that supplies the names for the list); page 67 (putting aside the wrongs of others to find our own mistakes); page 83 (the Promises that follow the amends work).

74ba25476da2.t: What is the difference between Step 8 and Step 9 in AA?

f6a79082b15a.t: Step 8 is the list and the willingness; Step 9 is the action. The Big Book treats them together starting on page 76, but Step 8 asks only that we write down everyone we harmed and become willing to make amends. No one is contacted until Step 9, which carries its own guidance about timing and about not injuring others.

b910d64974c0.t: What if I'm not willing to make amends to someone on my Step 8 list?

842630a623a4.t: The Big Book expects this and answers it directly: 'If we haven't the will to do this, we ask until it comes' (page 76). We put the name on the list anyway and pray for willingness rather than forcing it. Willingness often arrives gradually, one name at a time, and nothing in Step 8 requires us to act before it does.

68b64a79f943.t: Step 9 AA — Making Direct Amends | Big Book Guide

60aab72cd1f3.t: Step 9 AA explained from the Big Book: what direct amends means, how pages 76-83 walk us through it, and the Promises that follow on pages 83-84.

78509231ba26.t: The Step where we stop saying sorry and start repairing what we broke.

3d88dfdeb22c.t: Step 9 reads: "Made direct amends to such people wherever possible, except when to do so would injure them or others." By now the hard inventory work is done. Step 4 showed us the wreckage, Step 5 said it out loud, and Step 8 put names on a list and prayed for willingness. Step 9 is where all of that leaves the notebook. In Big Book terms, an amend is not an apology. An apology is words about the past; an amend is a repair made in the present. The book's own word is repair: "Now we go out to our fellows and repair the damage done in the past" (page 76). Money owed gets paid or arranged. Lies get corrected. People we hurt get faced.

27aac07438b3.t: Where Step 9 Lives in the Big Book

6463112b26a5.t: Step 9 belongs to Chapter 6, <0>Into Action</0>, and it gets more space than almost any other Step. Step 8 is handled in a single paragraph on page 76, and then the book spends pages 76 through 83 walking through amends situation by situation, with the famous Promises closing the discussion on pages 83 and 84. We are not doing this to look good or to be forgiven on schedule. As page 77 puts it, "Our real purpose is to fit ourselves to be of maximum service to God and the people about us."

7b7add059a56.t: The instructions read like a casebook. For the person we resent, or who resents us, we go in a helpful and forgiving spirit, admitting our part and never arguing theirs, because we are there to "sweep off our side of the street" (page 77). For the people we owe money, the book is blunt about avoidance: "We must lose our fear of creditors no matter how far we have to go, for we are liable to drink if we are afraid to face them" (page 78). We tell them what we are trying to do and arrange the best terms we can. For wrongs with serious consequences, even criminal ones, page 79 says we remember that we decided to go to any lengths, and "we ask that we be given strength and direction to do the right thing, no matter what the personal consequences may be."

8ee2b273d37c.t: Then comes the exception clause, and pages 79 through 81 treat it with real care. <0>Wherever possible</0> does not mean wherever comfortable, but the second half of the Step is just as binding. We never make an amend that creates a new victim. If the whole truth would wound a spouse or drag an innocent third party into the wreckage, we hold off, seek counsel, and find another way to set things right. Page 82 pictures the drinking alcoholic as "a tornado roaring his way through the lives of others," and Step 9 is meant to still the storm, not spin it up again. Manner matters too. Page 83 says we should be "sensible, tactful, considerate and humble without being servile or scraping." And we do not wait for perfect conditions: "The spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it" (page 83).

d4a07a059e8e.t: The Big Book attaches its most famous paragraph to this Step. "If we are painstaking about this phase of our development, we will be amazed before we are half way through" (page 83). What follows on pages 83 and 84 is the passage many groups read aloud at every meeting: a new freedom and a new happiness, no more regretting the past, fear of people and of economic insecurity leaving us, the growing sense that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves. The paragraph ends with a working condition, not a wish: "They will always materialize if we work for them" (page 84). Members who have worked this Step say the same thing: the amends we dreaded most set us most free.

757fec9a064a.t: Let's be honest about why this Step stalls. We are afraid of the faces, the slammed doors, the debts bigger than we remembered, the consequences we cannot predict. Some of that fear is realistic. The Big Book never promises a warm reception; it only promises that our side of the street will be clean when we walk away. Some people will not forgive us, some amends take years, and page 83 says some wrongs can never be fully righted, and we need not worry about those if we would honestly right them if we could. The freedom in this Step comes from our willingness and our action, not from the other person's response. That is why page 78 warns that the fear itself is the danger, because an alcoholic hiding from someone is an alcoholic getting ready to drink.

c4f3e7e98bd9.t: Step 9 clears the wreckage, and Step 10 keeps it cleared. Once the amends are underway, page 84 says we have "entered the world of the Spirit," and the book moves straight into the next Step: continuing to take personal inventory and setting new mistakes right as we go. If Step 9 is the great housecleaning, Step 10 is how we keep the house clean one day at a time.

8317effba9a9.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (the Big Book), 4th Edition: Step Nine listed on page 59; working instructions in Chapter 6, "Into Action," pages 76-83 (resentments and enemies p. 77, creditors p. 78, serious consequences p. 79, protecting others pp. 79-81, the tornado passage p. 82, manner and timing p. 83); the Ninth Step Promises, pages 83-84; Step Ten begins on page 84.

91c512af5a6c.t: What is the difference between an apology and an amend in Step 9?

0b2ae19b4091.t: An apology is words; an amend is a repair. The Big Book's instruction is to go out to our fellows and repair the damage done in the past (page 76), which means paying debts, correcting lies, and changing the behavior that caused the harm. Saying we are sorry may be part of it, but the Step asks for direct action wherever possible.

a5486ae687b2.t: What does 'except when to do so would injure them or others' mean in Step 9 AA?

9fa6fe85b371.t: It means we never buy our own peace of mind at someone else's expense. Pages 79 through 81 give examples where a full confession would wound a spouse or pull an innocent third party into the wreckage; in those cases we hold off, seek counsel, and find another way to set things right without creating new harm. Page 83 adds that some wrongs can never be fully righted, and we need not worry about them if we would honestly right them if we could.
